items.name: Readability
items.evidence: Names are clear (persisterRestore.ts, #restore, isPersisterRestoreResult). The public helper has a JSDoc, and the non-obvious paths have comments ("the restored state has already been adopted", isRestoring comment). Formatting matches the codebase. One nested ternary for status is minor.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: #restore calls this.setState({...state,...}) instead of adding the dedicated reducer action the conventions ask for. Public types use PersisterRestoreResult<any, any> and `value as any`. Single restore goes through Query.#restore while bulk restore merges in createPersister, so there are two paths.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: The persisted Partial<QueryState> is spread into state with no normalisation: counts, timestamps and status are not checked (the reference validates these). If data is undefined, the code throws the persisted error with no cache error callbacks. Symbol.for makes the marker forgeable across realms.

items.name: Restore path API contract
items.name_zh: 恢复路径 API 约定
items.evidence: createPersisterRestoreResult is exported, uses a symbol marker, skips onSuccess/onSettled and forces fetchStatus 'idle'. But it uses the generic setState action, not a dedicated restore action. Bulk restoreQueries uses its own merge path instead of sharing the Query restore application.

items.name: Existing persister contract preserved
items.name_zh: 保持既有 persister 约定
items.evidence: Plain data passes through the wrapped fn unchanged, and the PersisterResult type change only widens what can be returned. But persisterFn now returns a marker instead of data (an existing test had to change), and the queryObserver isRestoring change affects every caller, not just marker results.
